analysis.one_liner: Restores injured patients' right to sue medical device makers in state court over defective devices.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in July 2008 with 15 cosponsors and was referred to committee, where it died without a hearing or a vote when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed federal law so that FDA approval of a medical device could not be used to wipe out state-law claims by people injured by that device. At the time, courts were reading the Medical Device Amendments of 1976 as barring those lawsuits for devices that went through the FDA's easiest review route. The bill would have applied that change retroactively, to cases already filed. It never got a committee hearing or a vote before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients injured by defective medical devices — such as faulty heart defibrillators, implants, or infusion pumps — would regain the ability to sue the manufacturer for damages in state court, including for cases already pending when the bill took effect. Their families and state courts would likewise regain authority over these claims. Device makers would face liability exposure, which supporters argued would add a safety check on top of FDA review.

how_it_helps.text: Under the bill, federal device rules would no longer shield manufacturers from state damage claims, so a person hurt by a defective device cleared through the FDA's easiest review path could still sue.
The change would apply retroactively — treated as law since 1976 and covering any pending or later-filed case — reopening claims for people already injured.

analysis.who_pays: Medical device manufacturers would bear the cost: exposure to jury verdicts and settlements in state courts for devices that had been shielded by FDA preemption, plus the legal defense costs that come with product suits. Some of those costs could be passed to hospitals and patients through prices or by pulling products from the market.

drawbacks.text: The bill was written broadly — it preserved state-law damage suits against 'any person' for any human-use device — which device makers argued would expose FDA-approved products to inconsistent jury verdicts across states and could raise product costs or drive devices off the market.

Because the change would have applied retroactively (effective as if enacted in 1976, and to any pending or later-filed case), manufacturers faced expanded liability for products designed and sold in reliance on the previous legal understanding — an admitted cost even for supporters.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is meaningful: restoring the ability of people injured by defective devices to seek compensation in court, and giving companies an added financial reason to catch defects before sale. The cost is real but contested: device makers argue liability suits raise costs and can pull safe, approved products off the market, and critics of litigation generally note jury awards can be unpredictable. On balance, the bill addressed a narrow gap — lawsuits over devices cleared through the FDA's easiest review path — and it died without a hearing or vote, so no weighing of these tradeoffs ever happened in committee or on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate health committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and expired when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: The bill's entire recorded history is a single day: introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on July 31, 2008.
No further action was taken before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and bills not passed by the end of a Congress die automatically.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medical device makers keep the federal preemption defense against state damage suits, and no court claims for patients were reopened.

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it with the Senate Majority Leader acting on his behalf.

for.name: 15 Senate cosponsors (14 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.role: Cosponsors including Sens. Leahy, Clinton, Obama, and Sanders

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further recorded action on it — no markup, no hearing in the record — letting it expire with the Congress.

against.name: Medical device industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation that would roll back preemption of state damage suits over FDA-cleared devices.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 15 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent socialist from Vermont; no Republicans signed on, and the Democratic-run committee never took it up.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped away the preemption defense that keeps FDA-approved devices largely immune from state damage suits, exposing makers to jury awards for defective implants and pumps. That exposure would also have given companies a stronger financial incentive to catch defects before selling.

Plaintiffs' attorneys and injured patients would have regained a path to compensation that preemption had closed off. Patients gain directly; lawyers gain a professional fee stream tied to the same claims.
